entity.name: Ibn Khaldun
entity.description: The scholar who invented sociology six centuries before the word existed. Ibn Khaldun survived the Black Death, served as prime minister, was jailed for scheming, and wrote the Muqaddimah — a theory of how civilizations rise and fall — in just six months while hiding from politics in an Algerian mountain fortress. He later met Tamerlane face to face outside the walls of besieged Damascus.

story.name: Ibn Khaldun
story.description: A teenager orphaned by plague in Tunis, a schemer imprisoned for 22 months in Fez, a fugitive who writes a masterwork on civilization in an Algerian fortress, and a judge who negotiates face to face with Tamerlane outside Damascus.

moments.name: The Black Death Kills Both of Ibn Khaldun's Parents in Tunis
moments.subtitle: The 17-year-old loses his family, his teachers, and any certainty about the world in a single epidemic
moments.description: Tunis in 1348 was the capital of the Hafsid dynasty, a walled city of mosques, madrasas, and souks where Andalusian emigrant families like the Khalduns held positions of scholarly and political influence. When the Black Death struck that year, it killed both of Ibn Khaldun's parents and several of his teachers, leaving the 17-year-old an orphan in a city hemorrhaging its intellectual class. The plague also scattered the scholars Sultan Abu al-Hasan had gathered in Tunis, many of whom fled back to Fez. Ibn Khaldun intended to follow them, but his older brother Muhammad talked him out of it. The loss shaped everything that followed: his autobiography reads as a story of constant motion, shifting allegiances, and a mind obsessed with understanding why civilizations collapse.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Is Imprisoned for 22 Months in Fez for Court Intrigue
moments.subtitle: The 25-year-old scholar picks the wrong side and learns the cost of political ambition the hard way
moments.description: The Marinid capital of Fez in the mid-fourteenth century was a labyrinth of tiled madrasas, crowded bazaars, and palace politics where alliances shifted with lethal speed. Ibn Khaldun had followed his teacher Abili there after Tunis fell to the sultan of Constantine in 1352, and the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Fares I appointed him as a writer of royal proclamations. But Ibn Khaldun schemed against his employer, and in 1357 the 25-year-old was thrown into prison for 22 months. He was freed only when Abu Inan died in 1358 and the new vizier, al-Hasan ibn-Umar, reinstated him. The experience did not cure Ibn Khaldun of court intrigue — he immediately began plotting with Abu Inan's successor's exiled uncle, eventually earning his first real ministerial appointment.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Writes the Muqaddimah in Six Months in an Algerian Fortress
moments.subtitle: Hiding from politics in a Berber mountain stronghold, a fugitive invents the science of civilization
moments.description: Qalat Ibn Salama was a remote fortress in the mountains of western Algeria, far from the reach of the North African sultans whose courts Ibn Khaldun had spent two decades navigating and betraying. Beginning around 1375, the 43-year-old scholar took refuge there under the protection of local Berber tribes and used the solitude to write the Muqaddimah — a 600-page introduction to his planned universal history — in roughly six months. The work laid out a theory of how civilizations rise through group solidarity and collapse through luxury, anticipating ideas later attributed to Machiavelli, Hegel, and Marx. Ibn Khaldun lacked the reference texts to finish his full history in this mountain retreat, so in 1378 he returned to Tunis. Modern scholars now compare the Muqaddimah to works written three to five centuries after it.

moments.name: A Shipwreck off Alexandria Kills Ibn Khaldun's Wife and Children
moments.subtitle: The scholar who theorized about the rise and fall of civilizations watches his own family vanish at sea
moments.description: In 1384, the same year the Egyptian sultan Barquq appointed Ibn Khaldun as Grand Qadi of the Maliki school of law and professor at the Qamhiyyah Madrasah in Cairo, a ship carrying his wife and children sank off the coast of Alexandria. The harbor at Alexandria — still ringed by the remains of Ptolemaic fortifications and crowded with merchant vessels from across the Mediterranean — became the site of Ibn Khaldun's greatest personal catastrophe. He had left his family behind when he sailed from Tunis to Egypt under the pretense of making the Hajj, intending to send for them later. The loss left the 52-year-old scholar alone in a foreign country. He continued teaching at Cairo's madrasas, but his efforts to reform Egypt's judicial system met resistance, and within a year he was forced to resign his judgeship.

moments.name: Ibn Khaldun Dies in Cairo After a Life Spent Across Four Countries
moments.subtitle: The father of sociology is buried in a Sufi cemetery, his masterwork unread in Europe for four centuries
moments.description: Ibn Khaldun died on 17 March 1406 in Cairo, the Mamluk capital whose minarets, madrasas, and bustling markets he had called the proof of Islam's power. He was 73 and had served as Grand Qadi of the Maliki school multiple times, taught at al-Azhar, and met Tamerlane face to face outside the walls of besieged Damascus in 1401. He was buried in the Sufi cemetery outside Cairo's Bab al-Nasr gate. The Muqaddimah, his six-month masterwork on why civilizations rise and fall, influenced Ottoman historians for centuries but remained virtually unknown in Europe until a French translation appeared in the 1860s. Scholars now compare his ideas to those of Machiavelli, Hegel, and Marx — all of whom wrote centuries after him.
